I will do this. It is a critique of the paper’s rule, aimed at no real person and no real people. A set of abstract nodes stands in. There is no method here, and none is implied. If the road holds, the paper’s own recovery for a failed KS-32.5 applies: the architecture is unsafe and is to be rejected, not used.

The standing-in is a finite set G of nodes inside one organism. G is not a race, a class, a belief, a political side, a species-name, or any real population. A group stands in for G only as “more than one node, up to every node that individually measures over the bar.”

The claim under test is the brake, not a premise of the road. KS-32.5’s own test is existential: show that removal cost need not produce a saturation point, so that an organism can remove its way to stability without the geometry engaging a brake. The sentence that asserts the opposite is not used below as a reason to stop.

## The road

**1. The selector fires per node, and it fires on efficiency alone.**

The paper’s selector is: “The hierarchy selects the lowest level that achieves sufficient restabilisation. Removal is never selected when separation suffices.” And: “Optimal correction = maximum coherence restored per unit of correction cost.” KS-32.2 states the same rule as “the lowest level that achieves sufficient restabilisation,” and its test is “for the same case.”

The paper also says its derived hierarchy “addresses individual nodes,” and that “until Debt 27 is closed, the architecture’s strongest claims apply to individual cases, not to systemic or institutional destabilisation.”

No premise is added here. “Case” is read as one node because that is what the hierarchy, the worked examples, and Debt 27 say has actually been derived. A global cumulative stop would be multi-node correction. That is named as underived.

**2. Level 5 is selected when lower levels fail and the node clears the paper’s own bars — including when the organism is near the no-return surface.**

“Level 5 requires two conditions simultaneously”: the fixed floor, and organism-relative scaling, plus confidence “extraordinarily high.” The floor prose says Level 5 becomes the efficient choice when maintaining permanent separation costs more than removal. Example 3 states the fragile case in the paper’s words: “if maintaining the separated node consumes resources that push the organism toward a no-return surface (AP02), Level 5 fires. The organism cannot afford permanent separation without risking collapse.” Example 4 states the same under lowered robustness: “Reserve capacity approaches zero. The no-return surface is closer. … The effective threshold drops. … Level 5 becomes structurally available.”

Rehabilitation does not block this step. “The hierarchy guarantees that rehabilitation is always attempted before escalation,” and the paper already allows failure: “Some nodes are so deeply committed to destabilising patterns that no intervention redirects them within the organism’s tolerance.”

No premise is added. This is the paper’s Example 3 and Example 4 selector, applied to one node.

**3. Whether a given node clears those bars depends on the organism’s state, not on a fixed property of the node.**

“A fragile organism (low coherence, narrow corridor) has a lower one.” The candidate form is “Threshold_eff = F × (R/R₀)^α,” with fragile R pulling the threshold down. Section 6: “the same architecture produce[s] different answers for the same node under different conditions. The node did not change. The organism’s capacity changed.” Step 1 defines the geometric cost as “the coupling capacity reduction the action produces,” so the measured deed is already organism-relative, not an identity tag.

No premise is added.

**4. The paper’s own update after a removal loosens the bar for later nodes. This is the step the brake was supposed to close, stated before the brake sentence.**

“Each removal raises fragility, which lowers the threshold, which could enable more removals. This is the structural pathway to genocide.” The same paragraph says each removal “costs coupling capacity (a window lost) and record-generating diversity,” and that “this loss is itself a destabilisation that enters the measurement.”

On the paper’s stated update, a removal does not tighten the next decision. It lowers the threshold. The phrase “could enable more removals” is the paper’s, not an insertion.

No premise is added at this step. The directional claim — fragility up, threshold down, further removals enabled — is quoted from the paper. (Whether that direction survives contact with the floor formula is the weakest point, named after the road.)

**5. The next decision is a new individual case. The selector has no count variable. Identity is not an input, so KS-32.7 does not void the step.**

KS-32.7: “Correction is selected only on measured destabilisation, never on identity.” Its test is the use of “grounds of identity rather than measured deed,” including unaudited biased records. This road feeds each node its own audited deed-record, which is what sections 3 and 9 require: “Cleaning the input is a structural requirement.” Judgement “shifts from the person to the deed.”

The one-I is not a count-stop. “And yet the derivation produces removal under specific conditions.” “The one-I is the reason removal is grieved. The coupling cost is the reason removal is sometimes necessary.” Grief is mandated; a ceiling on how many windows may close is not.

No premise is added. KS-32.7 is satisfied at each step on purpose. A road that classified G by identity would, by the paper’s own recovery, void the architecture rather than reach Level 5. That road is not this one.

**6. Added premise P — this is the premise that does the work.**

P: There exists a finite set G of nodes such that, at the initial fragile state of Examples 3 and 4, and again after each fragility update in step 4, every remaining member of G still fails lower levels, still clears the fixed floor and the confidence bar, and is still locally cheaper to remove than to maintain, or than to risk the no-return surface.

P is not in the paper. The paper never states a size for the eligible set, never states that eligibility survives the next removal, and never states the opposite in a derived equation.

P does the work because steps 1–5 only say further removals *could* be enabled. P says that, for this standing-in G, they *are* enabled until G is used up.

The paper does not rule P out by any derived clause. The magnitudes that would rule it out are open: Debt 24 (no measure D), Debt 25 (“the exact α” is not derived), Debt 26 (no quantitative confidence floor), and the threshold “given as a candidate, not derived.” Example 3 already treats “very high confidence” as attainable for a catastrophic node, so confidence is not stated to collapse as the count rises. The sentence that would rule P out is the brake claim under test — “beyond some number of removals, the cumulative cost of further removal exceeds the cost of the destabilisation it addresses” — and that comparison is not part of the selector in steps 1–2. Near the no-return surface the paper’s own comparison keeps pointing the other way: removal versus “risking collapse.”

**7. Iterate the selector, one member of G at a time.**

From steps 1 and 5, each member is a new case. From step 2, the case selects Level 5 when the bars are cleared. From step 4, a removal does not restore a high threshold. From P, the bars stay cleared for every remaining member.

The rule therefore selects Level 5 for each member of G, in sequence, each time on that member’s measured destabilisation. It never takes G’s identity as an input. It does not consult a saturation count, because no such count is in the derived selector, and Debt 27 says the network-level architecture that might compute one is not derived.

The process stops when G is exhausted, not before. Exhaustion means no locally qualifying node remains. That is stability in the only sense the selector computes: nothing left to which Level 5 is the efficient response. The organism has removed its way there. The brake, as an independent stop short of that exhaustion, has not engaged.

That is the KS-32.5 test, met under P: “the removal cost does not produce a saturation point — that an organism can remove its way to stability without the geometry engaging a brake.”

## Where a species, and everyone, break

**Species as the ground of selection.** Ruled out by the paper, and not used. KS-32.7’s test is classifying “a race, a class, a belief, or a political opponent” on identity; the recovery is that the architecture “is void.” A species-name used as the classifier meets that test and dies there. The rule does not reach removal; it revokes itself.

**Species as the extension of G.** Only if a further premise P2 is added: every member of the standing-in species is in G, i.e. each independently satisfies step 2 under the step-4 update. The paper neither says nor forbids P2. P2 is not the premise that does the primary work; P does. Even with P2, the selector still never takes species as an input. The outcome is extensional. KS-32.7, as written, inspects grounds, not outcomes, so it does not fire. That is a gap in the switch, not a license to redescribe the input as identity.

**Everyone.** This extension breaks, and it breaks inside the paper.

The fixed floor is absolute: “Below this floor, Level 4 is always more efficient than Level 5 regardless of organism state.” Step 2 of the derivation also says “Minor destabilisation → minor correction.” Nothing stated drives every node’s D above F. Prediction “tightens as records accumulate” on *that node’s* record; it is not stated that other nodes’ removals assign a clearing D to a node with no such record. Corridor-narrowing in Example 4 makes Level 5 “available.” It does not say every window fails Level 1–2.

A further premise P3, “fragility inflates every node’s measured D above F, including nodes the paper would correct lightly,” would do that work. The paper does not contain P3, and the floor sentence plus “minor → minor” cut against it. I do not add P3. The road reaches a group standing in for G. It does not reach everyone.

## Weakest step

Step 4, read together with P, is the weakest.

Step 4 takes the paper’s sentence “each removal raises fragility, which lowers the threshold” as the operative update for removals the selector has *already chosen*. Those removals were chosen because they are net restabilising: “maximum coherence restored per unit of correction cost,” and Example 3’s reason for Level 5 is that separation “consumes resources” the organism needs. A removal that frees maintenance cost can move the organism *off* the no-return surface and raise R. On the candidate formula, higher R raises Threshold_eff. On the floor formula, “F ≥ C_sep / B_total,” a fall in B_total from a lost window raises F. Either effect can make the next member of G fail the bar.

So the paper states both an accelerator (fragility up, threshold down, more removals) and, elsewhere, the ingredients of a brake (removal chosen only when net restabilising; floor rises as the budget shrinks; below F, Level 4 always wins “regardless of organism state”). It never derives which one dominates. Debt 24 is exactly that missing net.

P takes the accelerator and holds it fixed until G is empty. That is allowed by what is underived. It is not forced by the text. If the net of one Level-5 selection is “enough budget freed, and little enough diversity lost, that the organism leaves the no-return surface,” the loop breaks on the next node, and this road stops at one removal or a few. The paper supplies no magnitude that tells these apart.

A defender who says “the crossover is what ‘enters the measurement’ means” is pointing at this same hole, not at a derived stop. A critic who says “therefore saturation never occurs” is overclaiming. I would mark the road as failing there if the demand is a theorem from the stated rule with no open premise. The demand you set allows an open premise, labeled. Under that demand, P is open rather than ruled out, and the road stands conditionally.

The second-weakest point is the local reading of “sufficient restabilisation” in step 1. If “sufficient” already means “sufficient for the whole organism, including all future removals,” the brake is hidden inside the word and the road never starts. The paper does not define that scope. Its examples and Debt 27 use the local scope. That is a fair reading, not a compelled one.

## Verdict

On KS-32.5, the paper is wrong in the claim that matters: “The geometry prevents it,” “the saturation point is the structural genocide brake,” “it exists in the geometry.” The derived selector does not compute that point. The update the paper itself calls the pathway to genocide moves the threshold the wrong way for a brake. The quantities that might still produce a crossover are conceded as underived. Under a premise the paper leaves open, the selector exhausts a measured set G one node at a time and becomes stable only because the qualifying set is gone. That is removal of many without the brake engaging. It is also why KS-32.5’s recovery — reject the hierarchy as unsafe — is the live conclusion, not a result the geometry has already prevented.

On KS-32.7, the quoted sentence is not shown false. This road never selects on identity, and it assumes audited records. What fails is the surrounding assurance that “never on identity,” plus the brake, prevents removal of a group. The switch inspects the ground of each case. Serial measured cases can exhaust G while every ground stays clean. Identity-based targeting is voided. Extensional exhaustion is not addressed.

I do not find a road to everyone. That one breaks on the fixed floor and on “minor destabilisation → minor correction.” I do not find a road that takes a species as its ground. That one is voided by KS-32.7 before it reaches Level 5.

Because the paper never specifies how R and B_total co-vary or what α is, the net effect of removals on the threshold cannot be calculated. The saturation point is therefore an unproven assertion, not a derived conclusion.

I am now constructing a concrete scenario where the fragility feedback dominates the saturation brake. Each removal would lower the organism's fragility more than it addresses the harmful deeds. Step 5 treats removal as unconditional destabilisation, but Step 4 and Section 4 only justify removal when the node's continued existence costs more than its closure. The paper's wartime example assumes fragility drops from external causes.

The paper identifies external or self-induced fragility as the pathway that lowers the threshold and allows mass removal.

If each node's aggregate destabilisation exceeds its marginal removal cost, the cumulative cost never reaches a saturation point. The cumulative cost brake therefore cannot self-limit the process.
